criteria.name: Mission concept and rationale — What will it do, who are the users, why is it needed?
criteria.reasoning: Clear mission goal, four quantified objectives, explicit users and their needs, and objectives traced back to user requirements. Well referenced to literature ([1]-[6]). Only minor gap: no discussion of why a new satellite beats existing missions (e.g. Sentinel-2).

evidence.quote: Give reef managers direct, repeatable observations of coral colour over the whole Great Barrier Reef
The satellite would be operated by the Australian Institute of Marine Science (AIMS). Its customers are the Great Barrier Reef Marine Park Authority

criteria.name: Project plan — How you plan to complete the assignment, including either a Gantt chart or a timetable and information sources you plan to use
criteria.reasoning: Gantt chart with task descriptions, explicit rationale linking plan order to mission logic, float, and a risk/contingency table with triggers and responses. Information sources table included. Robust and mission-integrated; only slight weakness is no stated weekly hour budget.

evidence.quote: Project work is divided into weeks in the Gantt chart in Figure 1, and each task is described below it.
The order follows the mission: the imaging requirements (objectives 1 and 2) fix the orbit altitude and local time, so orbit work comes before ground control
Table 1: Project risks and contingency plans.

criteria.name: Preliminary progress — Technical content and evidence of sufficient work done to date
criteria.reasoning: Verified hand calculations: a=6978 km gives T=5801 s (correct), 14.9 orbits/day, sun-sync inclination 97.8° at 600 km (correct), 24.2° ground-track shift using the sidereal day (correct). Results are interpreted (swath vs revisit trade) and tied to contingencies; STK tutorials and a scenario started. Clearly on track.

criteria.name: Report presentation
criteria.reasoning: Logical structure with clear headings, labelled figures and tables with captions, consistent formatting, professional tone, and in-text citations ([1]-[11]) matching the reference list. Writing is clear and concise throughout. Very minor: some references lack full titles/author detail.

technical_issues.issue: 10 m GSD weekly imaging of a 2300 km reef is a demanding requirement; data volume and downlink rate needed to meet the 24-hour delivery objective are not yet quantified (acknowledged as future work via contingencies).
Sun-synchronous orbit choice is not yet justified against local time of node, which matters for consistent illumination of colour-change detection.

overall: Excellent preliminary report: well-justified Australian reef-monitoring mission with quantified objectives and users, a robust contingency-aware Gantt plan, correct verified orbit calculations with interpretation, and polished presentation. Minor gaps in trade justification and downlink sizing.

feedback.summary: An excellent preliminary report. Your Great Barrier Reef monitoring mission is clearly justified with quantified objectives, explicit users, and good referencing. Your Gantt plan is robust, with contingency triggers and a clear rationale tied to mission logic. Your verified orbit calculations and STK start show strong progress, and presentation is polished. To reach the very top, strengthen trade justification (why a new mission over existing satellites) and quantify downlink/data-volume needs.
next_steps: Justify the sun-synchronous orbit choice against local time of node, since consistent illumination matters for coral colour-change detection.
Quantify the data volume and downlink rate needed to meet your 24-hour delivery objective for 10 m GSD weekly imaging of the 2300 km reef.
Add a brief comparison with existing missions (e.g. Sentinel-2) to explain why a new satellite is needed, and complete reference details (titles/author info) where missing.
